title: Rights-Request Engine for Rejected Applicants
one_liner: A consumer tool that files legally formatted data-access and automated-decision requests to employers' hiring systems, turning silent rejections into scores, reasons and evidence.
customer: Job seekers, starting in the UK and EU under GDPR Art. 15/22, then Illinois and California. They pay $12 a month or $29 per request pack. Secondary buyers are plaintiff-side employment firms and researchers who license opt-in aggregate data.
problem: Applicants send dozens of applications, get almost no replies and never learn why (HN: 65 applications, 3 phone screens, 0 interviews). New laws give people rights to see and contest automated screening, but nobody uses them because finding the right contact and format is a hassle.
solution: A browser extension logs each application (company, ATS vendor, date). After 30 days of silence it files a data-access and automated-decision request, tracks the one-month deadline, escalates to the regulator, and parses the response into a structured 'why I was screened out' report. Opt-in aggregate stats show which employers and ATS vendors auto-reject which profiles.
why_now: California's automated-decision regulations start binding in Jan 2027 and Illinois' AI-in-employment notice law took effect Jan 2026. The Mobley v. Workday collective action is live and AI resume screening is ubiquitous. Job-search desperation is at a peak, and EU/UK rights already work today.
revenue_model: Consumer subscription or per-pack fees, plus opt-in anonymised data and insight licences to labor economists, unions and employment plaintiff firms. Employer-side compliance-readiness upsell later.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators created rights but no practical channel, and that friction is the enforcement gap. The service converts individual rights into aggregate leverage: an employer receiving 500 requests per role starts giving candidates real feedback, and the request-and-response dataset becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Build a GDPR-only MVP (templates, deadline tracker) for UK/EU applicants in two weeks, with a UK data-protection solicitor reviewing the templates. Seed it in UK and EU job-search communities and HN at £9 per pack. Measure response rates and refine.

title: Rights-Cleared 1929-1963 Corpus for AI
one_liner: Join scanned mid-century books, magazines and newspapers to Copyright Office renewal records to produce provably public-domain text for AI training, with libraries paid a share and spared the scraper load.
customer: AI labs, foundation-model startups and fine-tuning shops that need litigation-proof training data, plus library and archive partners who supply scans (buyer is head of data or general counsel).
problem: Clean training data is now a legal necessity, but the best public-domain corpus (Harvard's Institutional Books 1.0, 983,004 volumes, 242B tokens) is largely pre-1929 text. For US works published 1929-1963, copyright lapsed unless renewed, yet renewals were rare (a 1961 Copyright Office study found fewer than 15% of registered copyrights renewed). The registration and renewal records exist but nobody has joined them to scanned text at scale. Meanwhile libraries are drowning in AI bots and have no sustainable way to offer their collections.
solution: Take scans that already exist (Internet Archive, partner libraries, HathiTrust-style holdings). Match each volume to Catalog of Copyright Entries registrations and renewals (Stanford renewal database for 1923-1949 books; Copyright Office online records for 1950+), and exclude foreign works restored under the URAA. Output a per-volume rights dossier with evidence links and a confidence score. Sell dataset snapshots with a signed provenance certificate (and insurance-backed warranty as revenue grows). Offer participating libraries a paid bulk-snapshot mirror (S3 or rsync) so AI buyers stop scraping their sites, with a revenue share.
why_now: The Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (2026-09-27) claim executives knew mass book piracy was illegal. Harvard and OpenAI/Microsoft-backed public-domain releases show buyers want clean data. Creative Commons (Aug 2026) says heritage institutions need standardized 'prosocial conditions' for AI access, and some (the National Library of the Netherlands, Trove) have closed access.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses ($25k-$250k per slice or annual refresh), provenance certificate fees, revenue share paid to libraries, bespoke rights-clearance projects for publishers reissuing out-of-print titles.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for legal AI text isn't scanning, it's rights determination: a huge band of 1929-1963 US works is public domain because nobody filed a renewal, and it's invisible until someone does the record join at scale. Libraries currently do this by hand. Evidence: Institutional Books 1.0 covers 983,004 volumes and 242B tokens (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08300). Wikipedia notes non-renewed pre-1964 works are public domain, the 1961 study, and the databases that hold the records (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_renewal). GLAM-E Lab survey: 39 of 43 institutions (91%) saw traffic surges, 69% of those blamed AI training bots, 74% deployed countermeasures, and robots.txt was largely ignored (https://glamelab.org/products/are-ai-bots-knocking-cultural-heritage-offline/). Creative Commons Aug 2026 on institutions closing access (https://creativecommons.org/2026/08/19/open-heritage-in-the-age-of-artificial-intelligence/). Authors Guild briefs, HN 626 points (https://authorsguild.org/news/ag-v-openai-top-execs-knew-mass-book-piracy-was-illegal/).
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick a narrow, high-value slice (for example 1950-1963 US trade, technical and hobby magazines where renewal was nearly nonexistent) and download the matching Internet Archive scans and renewal records. Days 10-25: run a first 5,000-volume join, have a copyright attorney sign off on the method and the URAA exclusions, and publish a free 500-volume sample with dossiers. Days 25-30: send the sample to 15 AI data buyers and licensed-data startups and to 5 mid-size libraries for a mirror pilot. Target one paid pilot in 90 days.

title: Booth-Day Cover: Weather-Out Insurance for Vendors
one_liner: A $5-$15 add-on at booth-application checkout that pays vendors their booth fee plus a loss tier when rain, wind, heat or smoky air wrecks an outdoor event day.
customer: Art-fair exhibitors, farmers' market growers, food-truck and craft-fair vendors, sold at checkout through event organizers and vendor-booking platforms.
problem: Vendors prepay $150-$900 in booth fees plus travel and perishable inventory. When an event is rained out, wind-cancelled, or smoke keeps customers home, organizers rarely refund, and event-cancellation insurance protects only the organizer. The vendor is the uninsured party, and smoke-driven closures are increasingly common.
solution: Per-booth-day parametric micro-policies triggered by hourly station and radar data (rain over a threshold during market hours, gusts above a limit, heat index/WBGT, AirNow/PurpleAir AQI at or above 151). Payout tiers of $75-$500 are set by booth fee. Cover is sold via API in the booking checkout. Organizers get a 'weather-safe vendors' badge, a revenue share and a dashboard. Claims are automatic and paid to the vendor's payout account.
why_now: Smoke seasons since 2023 made AQI-linked outdoor closures routine. Hyperlocal sensor networks and 1 km radar rainfall data are cheap. Embedded-insurance APIs make per-transaction cover easy to bolt onto checkouts. A likely very strong El Niño (CPC/IRI, September 2026) points to a wet winter in the southern tier, where winter markets and festival seasons run.
revenue_model: Premium of about $6-$12 per booth-day at a 20-30% loading over expected loss, with 15-20% shared with the organizer or platform. Later, multi-event season passes and organizer-side cancellation cover.
non_obvious_insight: In outdoor events the vendor is the uninsured party, and a booth-day is a near-perfect unit of insurance: known date, place, price and trigger. The checkout is the underwriting file and weather data is the claims adjuster, so there is almost no claims cost.
first_30_days: Pitch two or three regional market associations and one art-fair or festival platform. Underwrite through a parametric MGA. Ship a Stripe checkout link with a simple rain/AQI/wind trigger table. Pilot 100 vendors at about $6 each across fall festival season and publish the first payout story.

title: Service-Linked Loans for Vet Students Facing Caps
one_liner: Grad PLUS ended for new borrowers on July 1, 2026, and vet school now hits a $50K-per-year, $200K aggregate federal cap; clinics and rural practices can fill the gap with work-linked financing that doubles as retention.
customer: First- and second-year DVM students at high-cost programs (borrowers), and clinic groups, rural food-animal practices and state programs (employers who fund the retention hook).
problem: Veterinary medicine is one of 11 professional programs under the new caps, and out-of-state or private DVM costs can exceed $200K over four years, so students will lean on pricier private loans or cosigners. Meanwhile employers pay sign-on bonuses with no retention hook, and rural and food-animal practices cannot recruit; only 1.3% of vets are in food-animal practice, and South Texas is under strain from screwworm.
solution: A gap-financing product where employers pre-commit to fund a student's tuition gap in exchange for a 3-5 year service commitment with vesting forgiveness (like health-service scholarships). We underwrite, originate through a bank or CDFI partner, and administer vesting, recourse and state-incentive stacking, including Texas' funded rural veterinary incentive program.
why_now: The first cohort under the caps is enrolling this fall. Roll-ups are hungry for associates, Texas has funded rural vet incentives, and screwworm has made food-animal vet scarcity visible to policymakers.
revenue_model: 1-2% origination plus an annual administration fee paid by employers (8-12% of loan balance vested), and a spread on the loan book.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders see loan caps as a schools' problem. The second-order effect is that caps create a class of employers willing to pay to lock scarce DVMs four years early, turning tuition into the cheapest recruiting channel the industry has had.
first_30_days: Interview financial-aid officers at 4 high-cost schools. Sign term sheets with 3 employers (a rural practice group, a regional corporate group, a state program). Line up one bank or CDFI partner and get legal review on income-share and recourse rules in 3 states. Pilot with 10 students.

title: Half-Plate GLP-1 Menus for Independent Restaurants
one_liner: A menu-engineering kit that converts an independent restaurant's existing dishes into protein-first half-plates priced at about 65-75% of the full plate, to capture GLP-1 households that eat out smaller but still eat out.
customer: Independent and regional restaurants (10-60 seats, $1-4M revenue) in metros with a high share of higher-income Gen X and Boomer diners, paying $499 setup plus $99-149/month.
problem: Circana estimates 23% of US households now include a GLP-1 user and that these users will account for about 35% of food and beverage sales by 2030. Those households cut traditional retail food and beverage purchases, especially high-carb, high-sugar, refrigerated and frozen items, and shift toward protein, fiber, fresh produce and restaurant spending, yet they still outspend non-users. Big chains are chasing this, but independents have no menu-engineering staff. If they simply shrink portions at the same price, GLP-1 customers feel ripped off. If they shrink and cut the price proportionally, margins collapse.
solution: For each restaurant, a done-for-you overlay: 4-6 existing dishes re-specified as half-plates with protein grams, plate-cost and margin tables, pricing at 65-75% of full price to protect gross margin per cover, a small-plate 'protein first' section, and a nausea-friendly option (low-fat, low-volume). Deliverables include a printable menu insert, a QR page, POS/online-ordering item entries (Toast, Square, Clover) and simple local marketing via medspas, GLP-1 telehealth clinics and pharmacies that hand out a 'restaurants near you that fit your plan' card. Protein numbers come from recipe-level calculations, not vague 'healthy' badges.
why_now: GLP-1 adoption is at household scale (Circana, November 2025), and oral versions (Wegovy pill December 2025, Foundayo April 2026) plus cash prices as low as $149-$299/month on TrumpRx.gov are pulling in more users. Novo Nordisk is cutting list prices to $675/month in January 2027. Meanwhile restaurant spending is recovering, with independents beating national chains and Gen Z leading (BofA, August 2026), so independent owners are looking for a differentiator national brands cannot copy quickly.
revenue_model: $499 one-time setup, $99-149/month for menu updates, QR/landing page and local partnership marketing. Optional performance share (for example, $1 per redeemed 'plan card'). Later: bulk licensing to regional chains and food-service distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The obvious read is 'GLP-1 kills food demand'. The data says something different: users cut retail food but restaurant spending rises and total spend still exceeds non-users, so the demand shifts channel and portion size rather than disappearing. The winner is margin engineering (a half-plate that keeps dollars per cover), not a health-halo badge. Evidence: Circana (Nov 18, 2025) https://www.circana.com/post/glp-1-medication-users-to-represent-35-percent-of-u-s-food-and-beverage-sales-by-2030 and https://www.circana.com/insights-hub/glp-1s-consumer-behavior (23% of households, 35% by 2030, restaurants up, retail food down, users skew Gen X with income over $100K). Independents outperform chains: https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/restaurants-and-discretionary-spending.html . Caveat: the Circana pages I could read did not give the size of the restaurant-spend lift, so validate it with a few owners' POS data.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Walk in on 20 independent restaurants with a one-page free audit of their own top 5 dishes (protein grams, half-plate cost and price). Convert 5-8 into paid setups. In parallel, sign 2-3 medspas or pharmacies to hand out the plan card and track redemptions to build a case study. Target: 5 paying restaurants and one measurable uplift story (covers or check average on half-plates) by day 30.

title: Decoy Employees: Canary Tokens for People
one_liner: AI-run fake accounts-payable and help-desk staffers listed where attackers scrape, with voice agents that answer, harvest attacker infrastructure and alert the real team the moment anyone probes.
customer: Security teams at mid-market and enterprise companies in finance, healthcare and professional services, MSPs, and cyber insurers.
problem: Social-engineering crews research org charts and websites to find AP staff and help-desk numbers. Voice-deepfake defenses react only after the call, and defenders get no early warning that they are being targeted. Reports of successful voice-deepfake attacks are rising fast.
solution: Create decoy personas (an AP specialist, a help-desk line) that appear in the company's staff page, vendor portals and public contact lists, never on fake LinkedIn accounts. Each has a mailbox and a monitored voice agent that engages callers safely with no connection to real systems. Every contact triggers an alert with caller number, script, requested bank changes and voice samples, feeds the SIEM, and builds a weekly attack-tempo report for insurers.
why_now: Voice cloning and real-time voice agents make plausible fake clerks cheap. Vishing has surged and attackers automate reconnaissance, so deception is one of the few defenses that scales with attacker automation.
revenue_model: $1.5-3K per month per decoy set, MSP resale, and insurer partnerships.
non_obvious_insight: Canary tokens for files and credentials are standard, but canary employees are not. Decoys turn the attacker's reconnaissance into your telemetry, so the more the attacker automates, the more signal you get.
first_30_days: Build one persona pack with a voice agent and alerting. Deploy at 5 friendly companies with legal and HR sign-off, collect 30 days of hits as proof, and price a $1K per month pilot.

title: Tariff Refund Claim Files for Small Importers
one_liner: Turn a small importer's messy customs data into a refund-ready, financeable claim ledger, paid by success fee or on sale of the claim.
customer: US importers of record with roughly $50K to $5M of IEEPA duties who lack in-house customs staff, plus the licensed customs brokers serving them. Claim-buying funds and lenders are the second payer, paying a per-file diligence fee.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026 and the CIT ordered refunds. CBP's CAPE tool has accepted about $134.7B of the roughly $166B pool as of September 11, 2026. The tail sits with the smallest importers. Their ACE accounts are unapproved, they missed the 90-day request window, or their entries are liquidated beyond the 80-day reprocessing window, which the DOJ is appealing at the Federal Circuit. Phase 3, for liquidated entries, was slated for October 6 but delayed. Many are selling claims at deep discounts out of fear or confusion.
solution: Ingest ACE entry-summary reports, broker CSVs and payment records. Map every line to the IEEPA HTS 9903 lines. Compute per-entry phase eligibility, liquidation dates and protest deadlines. Flag duplicate or wrong importer-of-record entries, drawback and FTZ overlaps, and interest owed. Output CAPE-ready batches plus a chain-of-title 'claim data room' with a probability-weighted value for the appeal-dependent entries. A licensed broker partner files, so the product stays software plus workflow. The same engine reprocesses future tariff refunds and exclusions.
why_now: The window is open now: CAPE phases run through fall 2026, the Federal Circuit appeal will set the value of the liquidated tail, and hedge funds and lenders are already buying refund claims. Successor tariffs under other statutes create the same entry-level data problem next year.
revenue_model: 8 to 12% success fee on refunds recovered. A 2 to 4% origination fee when a claim is sold or financed. $500 to $2,000 per-claim diligence files sold to buyers. A subscription for customs brokers who use it across their book.
non_obvious_insight: Distressed-claims desks (Lehman, FTX, Celsius trade claims) know a claim's price is set less by the underlying merits than by documentation quality, chain of title and timing. Whoever standardizes the data room becomes the market's gatekeeper. The small-importer tail is mispriced because sellers can't prove what they are owed, and buyers can't underwrite what they can't verify. The moat is the underwriting file, not the filing.
first_30_days: Build an ES-003 and ACE CSV parser with two or three friendly licensed customs brokers. Offer a free 'refund gap audit' to 30 small importers found through public importer lists. Sign 10 on contingency. Get letters of intent from one or two claim buyers wanting standardized diligence files.

title: MCP Connectors for Emerging-Market Government Portals
one_liner: The maintained tool layer, with a human fallback network, that lets agents file taxes, e-invoices and registrations in Kenya, Nigeria, India, Mexico and Brazil.
customer: Bookkeeping and accounting SaaS, SME lenders, fintech onboarding teams and agent builders operating in Kenya, Nigeria, India, Mexico and Brazil.
problem: Agent tool ecosystems (MCP registries, Composio) index US SaaS APIs. In emerging markets the highest-value SME tasks, such as tax filing, e-invoicing, company registration and customs, live behind government portals with no API, monthly UI changes, captchas, OTPs and sometimes biometrics or paper stamps. Agent builders cannot reach 99% task completion, so agent products stall at the portal.
solution: Build and continuously test connectors (MCP servers) for Kenya's iTax and eTIMS, Nigeria's CAC and revenue-service portals, India's GST and MCA, Mexico's SAT/CFDI and Brazil's Receita and gov.br. Add a human fallback pool of cyber-cafe operators and licensed accountants who complete steps the agent cannot (consented OTP relay, captcha, in-person stamps). The buyer pays per successful filing, with a maintenance SLA.
why_now: The Ninth Circuit's 'the agent is the user' ruling and MCP's move to the Linux Foundation legitimize agents acting through user-authorized sessions. E-invoicing mandates (Kenya eTIMS, Brazil NF-e, Mexico CFDI, India GST) create recurring filing volume. Composio's $25M Series A shows the tool layer is fundable, and no one is building it for the Global South.
revenue_model: $0.50-3 per successful transaction, plus a monthly connector subscription per market ($200-1,000), plus a premium for the human-completion SLA.
non_obvious_insight: Connector maintenance is the moat because portals change monthly and nobody glamorous wants to own that. The human fallback converts 70% automation into 99% completion, which is exactly what fintech buyers pay for. The cyber-cafe operator, the old human middleman, becomes the agent's last-mile API.
first_30_days: Build Kenya iTax/eTIMS and Nigeria CAC connectors first. Sign three bookkeeping or SME-lending startups as design partners at a per-filing price. Staff the human fallback yourselves for the first 500 filings and log every failure type to prioritize automation.

title: Second-Life Studio: Shelved Human Drugs for Dogs
one_liner: Mine the wreckage of failed human biotechs for safe, clinical-stage molecules that make viable dog and cat drugs, and broker them to animal-health companies.
customer: Animal-health business-development teams (Zoetis, Elanco, Dechra, Boehringer AH, Merck AH, Ceva, Virbac) and venture-backed vet-drug startups pay for screening and deal flow. Sellers (liquidating biotechs, bankruptcy trustees, pharma pruning portfolios) pay success fees.
problem: Roughly 300 'zombie' biotechs exist, and 2026 has brought 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies. Their clinical-stage compounds, with human safety and PK data in hand, are being abandoned because human markets need $300M+ peak sales. Meanwhile animal health has few new molecules for canine lymphoma and osteosarcoma, feline CKD, IBD or chronic pain, and about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never get IV chemo.
solution: A scouting and licensing studio. It uses AI to mine ClinicalTrials.gov, SEC filings, layoff and bankruptcy trackers for discontinued assets that were not stopped for safety. It scores each for target conservation in dogs and cats, allometric dosing, market size and eligibility for FDA CVM expanded conditional approval. It packages dossiers with a vet development plan and KOL letters, then brokers options, licenses or asset purchases, keeping a finder's fee plus equity or royalty in each spun-out newco.
why_now: The supply of stranded assets is at a peak (layoff tracker, 300 zombies, wobbling software-only AI-drug shops like Schrodinger). Precedents are proven: verdinexor, a human-oncology-origin XPO1 inhibitor, became the first oral canine lymphoma drug, and anti-NGF antibodies moved from human programs into dogs and cats. Pet owners increasingly want oncology and chronic-pain options, while roll-ups (GoodVets, Mars) create channels that can absorb new products.
revenue_model: $15-25k 'Vet Opportunity Screen' reports per target class. $25-100k option fees. Finder's fees of 2-5% of deal value, plus 5-10% equity or royalty in spun-out veterinary newcos.
non_obvious_insight: The human 'failure' threshold is a commercial threshold, not a biology threshold. A $50M-peak product is a rounding error to human pharma but a real business in companion animals, where the target biology is often the same. Zombie boards will sell for pennies, so a tiny studio can option assets that incumbents ignore.
first_30_days: Build a database of about 500 clinical-stage assets terminated since 2019 for non-safety reasons, and shortlist 30 with plausible vet indications. Email 15 liquidating boards and 10 animal-health BD leads. Sell the first two $15-25k target-class screens as paid retainers. Aim for the first option agreement within 4-6 months.

title: Inherited-Rental Stabilization Service for Estate Attorneys
one_liner: A flat-fee 30-day service that stabilizes rental properties the moment an owner dies, sold through probate attorneys and trust officers who fear personal liability.
customer: Probate and trust-and-estates attorneys, professional fiduciaries and bank trust departments who represent executors and heirs of deceased small landlords. Attorney or fiduciary pays the flat fee out of the estate. Beneficiaries later pay ongoing management or sale-prep fees.
problem: The average small landlord is in their 60s or older, and a wave of these owners is dying and passing on 2-to-30-unit portfolios to heirs who have never landlorded. In the first 60 to 90 days after death everything degrades. Tenants get confused about who to pay and some quietly stop, so collections drop 20 to 40%. The named insured on the policy is dead and coverage gets contested or non-renewed. Security deposits, a legal liability that has to be accounted for in trust, are mingled into the deceased's personal account. Leases are undocumented handshake month-to-months, and vendors stop being paid. The attorney does not want to run a rental business but is exposed to a beneficiary surcharge claim if value leaks.
solution: A productized 'Day-1 Stabilization Package' delivered by a small field team and software. It has five parts. First, a tenant estoppel and 'pay here' notice with a new rent-collection account, sent within 5 days. Second, a rent-roll and lease audit, verifying every tenant, deposit and lease term against bank records. Third, deposit-liability reconciliation and a segregated trust account. Fourth, insurance re-papering: new named-insured and vacancy status filings. Fifth, a code-compliance and deferred-maintenance walk-through, with photos, for the estate inventory and stepped-up-basis appraisal support. The output is a court-ready fiduciary report the attorney can file. The last step is an option: convert to ongoing management at a preferential rate, or a sale-ready package for listing.
why_now: The great wealth transfer from boomers is reaching real estate now, and small individual landlords are among the oldest owner cohorts. Rising property values make each estate's rental portfolio high-stakes. Attorneys are reluctant to run operating businesses, and fiduciary surcharge risk is well understood. Large PM firms ignore 6-unit estates. Cloud rent collection and e-sign tools make a 30-day remote-plus-local process feasible for a tiny team.
revenue_model: $2,500 to $6,000 flat fee per estate (scaled by unit count), paid by the estate. About 30 to 40% of estates convert into ongoing management at 7 to 9% of rent, or into a listing or sale referral with a 1 to 2% fee. Bank trust departments can be sold an annual retainer.
non_obvious_insight: The best property-management clients are never won through marketing. They arrive through a death, and the person deciding who gets the call is an attorney who cares about liability, not price or software features. The attorney's real product need is documentation to defend against beneficiary surcharge claims, not better rent collection. The real revenue leak in the first 90 days is the 'ghost landlord' period, when tenants do not know who to pay.
first_30_days: Write the checklist and notice templates (a weekend of work if you have PM experience). Contact 30 probate attorneys and 5 corporate fiduciary or trust officers in one metro, offering a free 45-minute CLE-style talk on 'the first 90 days of an inherited rental portfolio' through the county bar's trusts and estates section. Offer a discounted first stabilization at cost to two attorneys for testimonials and case studies. Line up a bookkeeper and a local handyman for the field-work side and use existing PM software for rent collection.

title: Consolidation Shock Radar for Independent Clinics
one_liner: Every roll-up creates a wave of unhappy clients and departing staff near the acquired clinic; sell independents, would-be founders and lenders a radar that finds those neighborhoods first.
customer: Independent and affordable-care clinics (client win-back and recruiting), DVMs leaving corporate to open practices, and practice lenders or equipment lessors.
problem: GoodVets is buying WellHaven (75 to 116 locations, announced 2026-09-24), and Mars runs about 2,100 clinics. After a deal, prices, hours and staffing change, but nearby independents have no signal about where clients and staff are becoming loose. De novo founders pick sites by gut feel and lenders lack local competitive data.
solution: Track acquisitions using state facility records, Google Business Profile and website changes ('now part of...'), price-list scrapes, review-sentiment shifts and job-posting churn. Deliver (a) an alert plus a ready-to-send 'neighbor clinic' welcome campaign and records-transfer kit for independents within 5 miles, (b) recruiting lists of departing DVMs and techs, and (c) site-scoring reports for lenders and de novo founders.
why_now: Continuous roll-ups (GoodVets/WellHaven this week), visits reportedly falling three years running, and corporate chains structurally unable to cut price. Open web data plus LLM extraction makes the tracking cheap for a two-person team.
revenue_model: $199-499 per month per clinic by radius, $2-5K per de novo site report, and a lender API subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Consolidation is discussed as a scale story. The neglected consequence is local displacement: the buyer's own integration changes service and pricing at a known date, which opens a recurring window for competitors. That window is a sellable time-series signal nobody packages.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for 3 states. Identify 30 clinics acquired in the last 12 months. Cold-email 100 independents within 5 miles with a 'your neighborhood's acquired clinics' one-pager. Aim to sell 5 subscriptions at $299 per month.

title: Large-Load Water Tariff Desk for Utilities
one_liner: An advisory-plus-software desk that gives small water and wastewater utilities the tariffs, effluent valuation and contract terms to negotiate with data centers.
customer: Municipal water and wastewater utilities and councils near data-center clusters (Texas, Arizona, Ohio, Georgia, Wyoming, Nebraska), plus investor-owned utilities preparing rate cases (the 15 largest private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025). The utility pays.
problem: Step one: states restrict potable and groundwater for data centers. Step two: developers turn to treated effluent and offer take-or-pay deals under NDA. Step three: the small utility on the other side has no large-load rate class, no reclaimed-water price, no drought-curtailment priority and no analysis of downstream users who depend on its return flows. Electric utilities built large-load tariffs 12-24 months ago, and water is next.
solution: A 'Large-Load Water Tariff Toolkit': a cost-of-service model for a new large load, minimum-take and curtailment clauses, effluent valuation (including return-flow obligations), construction cost recovery, and reporting and audit clauses matching Texas and Australian rules. Entry product: a one-page 'your effluent is worth $X per acre-foot' for every discharge-permit plant within 30 miles of a data-center cluster, built from public discharge-monitoring data.
why_now: Texas froze ERCOT approvals on Aug 3, Ohio scrapped its general permit, and the Mississippi River states are drafting a compact. Regulators are asking who funds the extra infrastructure. Developers will sign deals in months, and the utility side has no playbook.
revenue_model: $30-150k fixed-fee engagements for tariff design and effluent valuation, SaaS for the cost-of-service model, and a success fee on an executed contract.
non_obvious_insight: The party with new bargaining power is the small wastewater utility, whose effluent just became an asset, but it is the least-staffed party in the room. Advising the weaker side of a deal is where the money is when the stronger side has all the lawyers.
first_30_days: Map all discharge-permit plants near known data-center campuses using public discharge and permit data. Produce 20 one-pagers. Email utility directors and city managers, and offer a free 45-minute briefing. Aim to close two paid engagements of $30-50k.

title: RoboManual: Appliance Manuals Written for Humanoids
one_liner: A licensed library of articulated digital twins and operating procedures (where to press, how the latch moves, how much force) for the 500 most common home appliances, sold to home-robot makers and to appliance brands that want their products to be robot-ready.
customer: Home and general-purpose robot companies and robot foundation-model labs (1X, Figure, Sunday-type startups, Tesla-adjacent teams, lab groups training manipulation policies). Later, appliance OEMs (dishwashers, washers, ovens, fridges) and retailers.
problem: Home humanoids ship into thousands of models of dishwashers, washers, ovens and jars. 1X's Neo, the first humanoid actually delivered to consumers, leans on remote human operators for tasks like laundry and dishes because robots do not know how to operate your specific machine. Appliance makers wrote manuals for humans; nobody owns the equivalent for machines: hinge axes, latch travel, button actuation force, timing and failure modes.
solution: A physical-measurement studio that scans and instruments appliances. It produces articulated 3D assets (URDF/USD) with annotated affordances (press points, required force, latch and door kinematics, common jams) plus step-by-step procedure graphs and video of human demonstrations. Delivered as a dataset license and a lookup API keyed by model number, so a robot can scan a label and retrieve its operating plan. Every deployed robot's failures feed back to update the manual. Appliance OEMs pay for inclusion and a 'robot-graspable' certification.
why_now: Consumer humanoids started shipping in 2026 (1X Neo, $20k or $499/month) and are teleop-assisted, so every learned procedure has a direct dollar value in removed operator hours. Sim-based training pipelines are hungry for articulated real-world assets. Industrial pilots by Figure, Agility and Apptronik make robot makers seek reusable object knowledge.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses of $25-100k per year per lab or robot maker, per-lookup API fees at scale, OEM inclusion and certification fees ($20-50k per product line), and custom scan projects.
non_obvious_insight: Robots do not lack general knowledge about 'a dishwasher'. They lack knowledge about this latch and this button lag. The moat is physical measurement labor plus fleet feedback, not AI, so big labs will not bother to build it early. It is the 'second manual' of the appliance industry.
first_30_days: Partner with a scratch-and-dent appliance outlet and a repair shop for scan access. Capture 50-100 top-selling dishwashers, washers, dryers, microwaves and ovens with photogrammetry, a force gauge and video of human operation. Produce cleaned articulated assets with affordance labels and sell a pilot pack to 2-3 home-robot startups at $25-50k.

title: Skill Rooms: Proctored Work-Sample Studios for Hiring
one_liner: Walk-in, device-free testing studios where candidates take a 90-minute employer-designed work sample under ID-verified proctoring, with a portable score that many employers honor.
customer: Staffing firms and mid-size employers hiring entry and mid-level roles (customer support, analysts, junior developers, paralegals, sales development) who are drowning in AI-written applications and AI-assisted interview cheating. Employers pay $75-200 per sitting, candidates pay nothing.
problem: Resumes and cover letters are now noise. In a dataset of about 19,000 live interviews from mid-2025 to early 2026, over a third of candidates showed signs of AI-assisted cheating (close to half in software engineering). Google, Cisco and McKinsey have brought back in-person rounds, but each employer improvising its own on-site test is expensive.
solution: Studios in 10 metros, rented after hours from coworking spaces and community colleges. Fixed-time sittings with ID checks and locked-down machines, and standard job-family work samples (writing under time limit, spreadsheet modeling, code on an air-gapped machine, mock client call), scored by rubric with human review and AI assistance. Candidates get a 'Verified Work Sample' credential valid for 12 months and portable across employers, and employers receive pre-screened slates.
why_now: AI cheating in remote interviews is now measurable and widely reported, in-person verification is returning at large employers, and entry-level applicant floods make cheap, trustworthy screening valuable. Existing proctoring vendors (OnVUE and similar) focus on certification exams, not hiring work samples.
revenue_model: Per-sitting fee from employers, premium pricing for custom work samples, per-hire placement fees through staffing partners, and optional paid practice tests for candidates.
non_obvious_insight: When signals get cheap, standardized proctored tests win, which is how the SAT displaced recommendation letters. The portable score, not the room, is the business: every additional employer that honors it lowers each candidate's cost of proving skill and raises its value, and it gives displaced or credential-less workers a way to prove themselves without a degree.
first_30_days: Rent a 12-seat room in one city and sign 5 staffing agencies hiring for three roles. Design three work samples and rubrics, then run a first cohort of about 40 candidates. Charge employers $125 per candidate who passes, and use the results to sign the next 10 employers on the same score.

title: Accessibility Disclosure Kit for US Independent Hotels
one_liner: A phone-based room-measurement kit that produces the accessibility details federal law requires on booking pages, before serial plaintiffs sue.
customer: US independent hotels and small groups of 30-300 rooms, franchisees, and the ADA-defence law firms who refer them.
problem: The federal hotel reservation rule (28 CFR 36.302(e)) requires booking systems to give enough detail about accessible rooms for guests to judge suitability, yet most sites just say 'ADA room'. Serial-filer suits repeat across the same properties and cost thousands each to settle. AI booking assistants also need structured answers on step-free showers and bed heights.
solution: A staff app guides a 20-minute walkthrough per room type using phone measurement and photos (door widths, turning space, shower type, bed height, grab bars). It generates compliant descriptions and a structured feed for OTAs, Google and AI assistants, then monitors listings for drift and provides a litigation-readiness pack.
why_now: Hotels are now being listed in AI assistants that demand structured attributes, and phones with depth sensing make measurement cheap. Serial-filer litigation continues, which gives the wedge and the budget.
revenue_model: USD 600-1,500 one-time per property plus USD 25-60 per month for monitoring, with rev-share to referring law firms.
non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit gets you the budget and the structured data is the moat. Detailed accessibility data is the missing input for agent booking, and accessible travel is an underserved segment.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 ADA-defence firms. Run a free scan showing what a serial filer sees on 100 hotel websites as lead-gen, and sell a USD 499 audit to 20 properties.

title: Hour-Meter Forensics for Used Farm Equipment
one_liner: An independent inspection and identity report for used tractors and combines that cross-checks engine-hour logs across ECUs, serial numbers and liens to catch rolled-back hours and phantom sellers.
customer: Used-equipment dealers and auction houses, equipment-finance lenders and Farm Credit associations, and farmers buying $100K-800K machines on classifieds and marketplaces.
problem: Used machine value is driven by hours. Tools that roll back hour meters and ECU logs are openly sold, and buyers wire deposits to fake sellers. Lien and ownership checks are patchy. Row crops are projected to lose money for a fourth straight year and farm bankruptcies are up 19%, so lenders care about collateral and farmers buy used. Historically independent shops could not read OEM diagnostics, so no neutral party could verify a machine's history.
solution: Mobile mechanics with OEM-capable diagnostic tools pull hour counts from every module (engine, transmission, monitor, telematics) and compare them, review calibration and replacement logs, and flag mismatches. An identity module checks the serial against photos, runs a UCC lien search and does seller KYC, with escrow released on inspection. Output is a signed 'Hours Verified' certificate, later an API for lenders and auction platforms.
why_now: Deere's $99M settlement obliges it to open its diagnostic and repair tools for 10 years, creating independent access to the machine's real history for the first time. Repair restrictions cost farmers about $4.2B a year. Squeezed farm incomes push demand toward used machines, and leaked ID data feeds synthetic seller identities.
revenue_model: $195-495 per inspection paid by buyer or lender, $99 per lot from auction houses, a 0.5-1% escrow fee, and per-collateral fees from lenders for portfolio audits.
non_obvious_insight: Right-to-repair created a security market. Once independent shops can read what a machine really did, its history becomes a verifiable identity, a Carfax-like asset that OEM dealers, who profit from service and trade-ins, are structurally reluctant to publish. Whoever publishes trusted hours first owns the data asset.
first_30_days: Hire two ag mechanics who already own diagnostic tools. Offer a $150 'Hours Check' at three auction houses and five independent dealers during fall auction season. Publish the discrepancy rate as a case study. Then pitch equipment-finance lenders and Farm Credit associations a free 30-machine collateral audit.

title: Data Estate Broker for Main Street Closures
one_liner: An appraisal-and-brokerage service that finds, de-identifies and sells the operational exhaust (quotes, work orders, dispatch logs, inspection records) of retiring or closing non-tech firms to AI buyers.
customer: Owners, business brokers, insolvency practitioners and CPAs handling closures of small manufacturers, freight brokers, insurance agencies, energy contractors and engineering firms. The buyers are vertical-AI startups and labs that need real workflow data.
problem: Failed-company data is now valuable. Google bought bankrupt Spirit Airlines' data for $10M: 100M emails, 30M+ recorded calls, 763,000+ flights of ops data, 1.2M fuel slips and 787,452 parts purchases. Mercor was the underbidder. But SimpleClosure, the main shutdown broker, only serves VC-backed startups, whose H1 2026 shutdowns were 27.3% B2B SaaS and 14.4% AI. Buyers say they want scarce data from manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services and logistics. Those firms close or retire constantly and have nobody to appraise or sell their data.
solution: Start with operational, non-consumer-PII data, which is the least legally fraught. Examples are work orders, quotes and bids, dispatch and routing logs, inspection and maintenance records, CAD revision histories, and internal Q&A threads. Run a 'data asset scan' ($500-1,500, credited against fees), then rights review and de-identification. Package the results as licensed corpora, run a sealed-bid sale to vertical-AI buyers and take a 25-35% success fee. Recruit business brokers, liquidators and trade associations as referral partners. Consumer call recordings and customer emails are excluded until counsel signs off.
why_now: Buyers proved a price in Aug 2026 (Spirit, $10M) and there is a losing bidder waiting. SimpleClosure's own asset report shows buyers paying tens to hundreds of thousands for unique corpora and wanting 'how real work actually got done.' Vertical AI agents for trades and logistics need training data that does not exist on the open web. Small-business retirements are a multi-year wave, and Sherline Tools going out of business (Sept 2026) is one example.
revenue_model: 25-35% success fee on data licence sales, plus a $500-1,500 appraisal fee credited against it. Optional recurring 'living licence' fees for firms that stay open.
non_obvious_insight: The market for dead-company data exists, but the only broker is aimed at software startups, while buyers explicitly want boring industries. Evidence: Google's $10M Spirit purchase with Mercor as underbidder (https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/18/google-buys-crashed-airline-spirits-data-at-auction-because-ai/5288962). The HN discussion notes that Scale, Surge and Mercor are recreating workplace data (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49343559). SimpleClosure's asset report lists 'manufacturing, energy, banking, insurance, professional services, logistics' as scarce-data buyers (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/what-your-assets-are-worth/). Its H1 2026 report shows its funnel is startups (https://simpleclosure.com/blog/insights/state-of-shutdowns-h1-2026/). The main risk is privacy backlash. HN commenters doubt the de-identification ('I'm skeptical it'll be wiped correctly'), so the wedge is operational data with no consumer PII.
first_30_days: Week 1: pick two verticals, for example machine shops and freight brokerage. Book 20 calls with business brokers and CPAs who handle closures. Weeks 2-3: sign 3 exclusive listing agreements on a free data-asset scan. Line up 5 buyer LOIs from vertical-AI startups building quoting or dispatch agents. Week 4: complete one appraisal, get a privacy-counsel template for rights review, and run the first sealed-bid process.

title: Secret-Shopper Audits of Government Algorithms
one_liner: Submit synthetic applicants and questions to public benefits systems, chatbots and eligibility tools to measure real error and denial rates, then sell the evidence.
customer: State auditors and legislative oversight offices, legal-aid funders, civil-rights litigators, and government AI vendors that want an independent seal before a contract renewal.
problem: State and local buyers cannot audit the AI they bought, and no one owns post-award monitoring. Michigan's fraud detector wrongly accused 40,000 people and cost $20M plus $78M for a replacement. Contracts run 7 years with only 3% of provisions covering cybersecurity.
solution: Run agent-driven synthetic-case testers against public-facing eligibility screeners, 311 and permit chatbots, and (with authorization) internal decision tools. Publish error-rate and disparity reports with reproducible test cases. Offer a continuous monitoring subscription to buyers.
why_now: Cities and counties have moved from pilots to production AI, and the Glass/Sourcewell marketplace pilot covers about 120 agencies. Agentic testers are cheap in 2026, and Michigan makes the harm undeniable.
revenue_model: $30-120K per audit engagement, $5-15K per month for monitoring, and grant-funded public-interest audits. Vendors pay for certified re-tests.
non_obvious_insight: Public-interest audit funders and state auditors already have budgets and mandate but no measurement tool. The synthetic-case method needs no vendor cooperation and no data access.
first_30_days: Run a free audit of 10 public-facing city or state chatbots and publish the findings. Send the report to state auditors and legal-aid funders. Sign one paid audit from a funder or auditor.

title: Licensed True Stories for Narration Channels
one_liner: A story studio that interviews real people about real events and licenses the recordings and scripts to faceless story-narration channels, replacing scraped Reddit posts and fake AI-written 'confessions'.
customer: Operators of faceless YouTube, TikTok and podcast channels that narrate AITA-style, revenge, workplace and relationship-drama stories, from solo operators to 10-person studios, plus audio-drama and story apps. They pay roughly $40-$150 per non-exclusive license.
problem: These channels' supply is scraped Reddit posts they don't own, since authors keep copyright and Reddit's data licenses go to AI firms, not YouTubers. YouTube's July 2025 'inauthentic content' rules specifically flag readings of material not created by the uploader and templated narrated stories, and in January 2026 YouTube terminated 16 channels with 35M combined subscribers. Mods keep banning reposts and fabricated or AI-written stories, so fresh, real material is drying up. Freelancers on Fiverr write fake 'Reddit stories' for $10-$30 that read as obvious slop.
solution: A 15-minute voice-interview app plus a human editor. The storyteller tells their story out loud, and the studio transcribes and structures it into a narration-ready script with a signed release, ID check and revenue share. Channels get a non-exclusive or exclusive license and a 'voice-verified first-person account' provenance certificate they can show as original-source proof. Authors earn a share of licensed views through tracked license codes. Storytellers are recruited off Reddit so mods aren't disrupted.
why_now: YouTube's inauthentic-content policy took effect on 15 July 2025 and was followed by the January 2026 termination wave, so channel operators now need defensible originality and provenance. At the same time AI-written fake stories have flooded the genre, and mods removing them has shrunk the pool of scrapeable real material.
revenue_model: $40-$150 per non-exclusive license, $300-$800 for exclusive first-run, and bundles such as $499 per month for 10 licenses. Authors get 40-50% of revenue. Later, sell format and option rights to audio-drama and TV producers.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers are not short of scripts but of defensible originality. People tell true stories brilliantly out loud and badly in writing, so the audio-interview format both raises quality and creates a provenance signal that a text LLM can't cheaply fake. Mods know the top-performing genres and that the people who post these stories mostly do it for validation, not money, so a paid $30 interview is an easy yes.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 storytellers through Facebook groups, Craigslist and small creator ads at $30 per story. Produce 60 scripts with Whisper transcription plus human editing. Sell a $199 pilot pack of 10 stories to 20 narration-channel operators, found through public channel emails and faceless-creator Discords. Ask for view data on the first videos to validate the revenue-share model, and use the results as the pitch for subscription bundles.

title: Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers
one_liner: Independent pharmacies hold the half of the PBM ledger that employers never see, which is what the PBM actually paid the pharmacy. Pool it to run spread audits for self-insured employers, and give pharmacies a stay-or-leave calculator for their take-it-or-leave-it PBM contracts.
customer: Two sides. First, independent pharmacies, at $99-199 a month for benchmarking and a network-contract modeler. Second, self-funded local employers, school districts, counties and union funds (from 100 to 5,000 lives), plus the benefit consultants and TPAs that serve them, who pay per audit or a share of verified savings.
problem: The employer sees only what it paid the PBM. The PBM sees both sides and hides one. The pharmacy sees what it was paid and what it paid the wholesaler, but has no benchmark and no idea whether the network offer that arrives every Q4 for January 1 is worse than its peers' terms. Everyone negotiates blind. PBMs threaten a pharmacy with losing about a quarter of its business if it declines, and a plan sponsor cannot verify 'pass-through' claims.
solution: Read-only ingestion of the pharmacy's 835 remittance files and invoice costs from its pharmacy management system (PMS). Output 1) per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement benchmarked against NADAC and an anonymized peer pool. 2) A stay-or-leave model of each 2027 network offer built from the pharmacy's own claims mix. 3) With sponsor consent, a claim-level tie-out of the pharmacy-paid amounts against the employer's PBM claims file. That yields a true spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member, delivered as an audit the employer can use to renegotiate or move to a transparent PBM.
why_now: The contract season for January 2027 is happening right now, which gives a hard deadline and a free entry wedge. Employer fiduciaries are under pressure from ERISA suits over PBM costs, state PBM transparency laws and FTC scrutiny. Pharmacy closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores) have given local officials political will. OCR and LLM parsing of messy remit PDFs now makes onboarding a one-day job rather than a consulting project.
revenue_model: Pharmacy subscription of $99-199 a month, or free in exchange for data. Employer audit fees of about $8k-25k per mid-size sponsor, or 10-20% of first-year verified savings. Data licenses to state employee plans, attorneys general, employer coalitions and consultants at a higher tier.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in the PBM fight holds half a ledger, and only the pharmacy can prove the gap. Thirty pharmacies in one county reconstruct the local school district's and county government's spread at claim level. Independents will hand this data over willingly because it is the first ammunition they have ever had against take-it-or-leave-it contracts.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 pharmacies through the state independent pharmacy association with the pitch 'we will model your 2027 PBM offers free'. Build parsers for the three biggest PBMs' remit formats (the 835 EDI standard helps). Deliver the first stay-or-leave reports. Hire a healthcare attorney to structure data-use terms, since provider-manual confidentiality clauses and HIPAA de-identification are the main risk. Offer one local school district or county a free pilot spread audit and turn the result into a one-page case study.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Public Buyers
one_liner: A contingency-fee audit that finds 'tariff surcharge' line items on city, school-district, transit and university purchase orders and recovers the share vendors are now being refunded after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs.
customer: County and city finance departments, school districts, transit agencies, public universities and public hospitals. They pay 20-30% of dollars recovered and nothing upfront.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. Roughly 330,000 importers paid about $166B, and as of July only about $86B had been repaid, so about $80B remained outstanding. Refunds go to the importer of record, not to the public buyers who paid vendor surcharges (one machine-shop supplier surcharge was 2.7%). Small importers and delivered-duty-unpaid shipments, including many university and hospital equipment imports, are likely to go unclaimed. Brokers are paid per entry and have no reason to chase this.
solution: Step 1: mine open-checkbook portals to rank vendors in tariff-exposed categories (school buses, HVAC, lab equipment, IT, furniture, playgrounds) and file public-records requests for their invoices to find surcharge lines. Step 2: send standardized pass-through refund claims and negotiate credit memos where the contract or surcharge language supports it. Step 3: where the public entity was itself importer of record (DDU), file its own refund claims. A dashboard tracks vendor refund status and the client's recovered dollars.
why_now: Refunds are flowing in phases now, with liquidated-entry and AD/CVD cases coming later, so vendor cash is fresh but memory of surcharges will fade. Claim deadlines and statutes of limitation close within 12-18 months. Public entities are under budget pressure and readily accept no-cost recovery audits, as with utility-bill and sales-tax audits.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered dollars, with a lower fee on refunds recovered by filing as importer of record. The same platform later runs recurring price-escalation monitoring for a subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The money sits with a party who has no incentive to hand it over, while the party who bore the cost has unusual leverage: public buyers can demand transparency, make supplier performance part of the record, and threaten future award eligibility. Public procurement contracts and open-checkbook data make targets findable without any client cooperation.
first_30_days: Pull open-checkbook data for 3 states, file about 30 public-records requests for surcharge invoices, and have counsel review a standard claim letter. Cold-email 20 finance directors with a personalized 'you likely overpaid $X to Vendor Y' one-pager and sign two pilots on contingency.

title: PFAS Turf Audits and Replacement Planning
one_liner: Field-by-field PFAS and regulatory risk audits plus replacement bid packages for school districts and parks departments with aging synthetic turf.
customer: School district facilities directors, athletic directors, municipal parks and recreation departments and colleges.
problem: Thousands of synthetic fields installed in the 2010s are reaching end of life just as PFAS rules bite: New York's ban on selling PFAS-containing turf takes effect December 31, 2026, California's restriction on PFAS in covered surfaces began January 1, 2026, and other states (New Jersey, Maine) have bills to pause purchases. Districts do not know what is under their fields, may not be able to buy what they always bought, and face bond votes and parent pressure.
solution: A $2.5-8k audit per district: field inventory (age, product, manufacturer), lab testing of fibers and infill through an accredited partner, legal exposure summary, lifecycle-cost comparison of synthetic, PFAS-free, hybrid and natural grass, and turnkey bid documents; then project-management and referral fees.
why_now: 2026 effective dates, active parent and environmental groups, and pending state bills create urgent, budgeted decisions.
revenue_model: $2.5-8k audits, testing pass-through margin, 2-4 percent project-management fees on $500k-1.5M projects, supplier referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody owns 'what is my turf made of' data and manufacturers will not volunteer it. Sitting between district, lab and contractor makes you the neutral spec writer who controls the RFP.
first_30_days: Build a public-records inventory of turf fields in New York from bond documents and board minutes, pitch 50 districts, line up an accredited lab, and sell three audits.

title: Vet-Prescribed Walks for Post-Surgery and Senior Dogs
one_liner: Certify dog walkers to deliver vet-written controlled-walking protocols after cruciate and spinal surgery, and to send structured mobility reports back to the clinic.
customer: Owners of dogs recovering from orthopedic or spinal surgery (TPLO, luxating patella, IVDD) and owners of senior arthritic dogs. Referral partners are surgical and rehab vet practices, who get reports at no charge.
problem: Discharge sheets say things like '5-minute leash walks four times a day, add 5 minutes a week,' and working owners cannot do it. Dogs get over-exercised or under-exercised and some re-tear the repair, which is a $4k to $6k mistake. Most walkers are afraid of the liability, and most vets don't trust an unspecified walker to follow a protocol. Meanwhile arthritic seniors decline slowly and owners miss it, while the walker sees the hesitation at stairs and the shorter walks first.
solution: A short walker certification (protocol cards written with two partner rehab vets, sling and non-slip handling, escalation rules). Visits are timed, leash-controlled, and followed by a structured report covering minutes walked, a 0 to 4 gait score, stiffness on rising, toileting, and a 15-second weight-bearing video. The report goes to the owner and the clinic ahead of the 2, 6, and 8 week rechecks. Red flags (swelling, heat, toe-touching) trigger a same-day call. A senior SKU gives a monthly mobility check with a gait video and pain questionnaire, so owner and vet can see whether joint meds or the newer arthritis injectables are actually working.
why_now: Vets are short-staffed and cannot run rehab follow-ups themselves. Pet insurance adoption keeps growing, so owners protecting a multi-thousand-dollar surgery will pay for compliance. The newer arthritis injectables raised the need for objective at-home response tracking, and safety debates around them make vets want data. Return-to-office pushes more owners out of the house all day right when recoveries need multiple short visits.
revenue_model: Post-op bundle of roughly $900 to $1,800 over 6 to 8 weeks (short visits at $30 to $45), with the walker keeping about 70 percent. Walker certification fee of roughly $250 to $300. Senior monitoring subscription at about $39 a month. No referral kickbacks to vets, so it stays clean; clinics get the free reports and fewer failed recoveries.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable clients in this business are not the healthy dogs on the schedule, they are post-op and declining dogs, because the protocol needs several short, geographically tight visits a day and the owner is desperate. The gap is trust, not supply: a protocol and a report format turn 'a walker' into a rehab extender that vets will refer to.
first_30_days: Sit down with the techs at two local surgical or rehab practices and write a one-page walking progression with them. Get yourself and three walkers through a dry run. Offer the first 10 post-op dogs a reduced bundle in exchange for report feedback, using a simple form that generates a PDF. Ask each clinic to slip a card into TPLO discharge packets and track how many convert.

title: PFAS Test-Result Exchange for Small Brands
one_liner: A members' data pool where small brands share lab results indexed by supplier, material lot and SKU, so nobody pays $500+ to test the same fabric or coating twice.
customer: Product-compliance managers at small and mid-size apparel, outdoor, cookware, cosmetics, textile and food-packaging brands and importers ($5M-$200M revenue) selling into US states with PFAS product laws and into the EU.
problem: PFAS rules are fragmenting through state product bans and reporting laws, EU packaging limits and a pending EU universal restriction (all unverified in the briefing; re-check current status). Supplier declarations fail because suppliers often do not know what is in their coatings. Testing costs hundreds of dollars per sample, and small brands that buy from the same mills and coaters each test alone. 'PFAS-free' marketing claims also draw class actions.
solution: A neutral cooperative. Members upload lab PDFs, which are parsed automatically and tagged to supplier, mill, material spec and date. The exchange scores confidence per supplier-material ('3 independent labs, 12 samples, all under threshold'), flags outliers, recommends where a new test buys the most certainty per dollar, negotiates group lab rates, and generates the state or EU evidence file. Contributions earn credits.
why_now: State PFAS product deadlines and EU packaging PFAS limits are landing in 2025-26 (background, verify), total-fluorine screening is cheap enough to run routinely, and LLM parsing turns messy lab PDFs into structured data.
revenue_model: Membership of $3-15k/year by revenue tier, pay-per-query for non-contributors, a 10-15% margin on group lab testing, and a paid 'independently verified' badge program.
non_obvious_insight: Declarations fail through ignorance, not malice, so the durable defense is measurement. Measurement is a shared-cost, non-competitive good, like a credit bureau for materials. Antitrust risk is low if the pool holds test data only and never pricing.
first_30_days: Partner with one accredited lab and one trade association (outdoor or apparel). Recruit 10 founding members who contribute 200+ historical lab reports, stand up a spreadsheet-backed MVP with parsed PDFs, and charge a $2.5k founding fee.

title: Robot Gymnasium Inside a Dead Mall
one_liner: Lease dying mall wings for pennies, stage them as real-world sets, and rent them by the day to robotics startups that need diverse places to collect training data.
customer: Humanoid and manipulation-robotics startups (seed to Series B, 20-200 people) and robot-data vendors. They need varied real environments, teleoperator labor and QA'd data, and they can't build a facility of their own.
problem: Robot foundation models are data-starved. Collecting demonstrations needs varied, realistic settings such as grocery aisles, pharmacies, kitchens, hotel corridors, escalators, elevators and glass doors. Lab space in tech metros is tiny and expensive. At-home gig collection is cheap but noisy and raises privacy issues. Chinese players are building 10,000+ m2 collection campuses, and the US has almost nothing comparable.
solution: Take a short-term license on 30-100k sq ft of a dead mall, often at $0.25-1/sq ft because the owner's alternative is a vacant box. Build 8-10 modular sets from closed-store fixtures and thrift furniture: grocery aisle, pharmacy counter, apartment kitchen and bedroom, laundromat, hotel hallway, office. The mall's escalators, revolving doors, elevators, tile and carpet changes and glass storefronts come free as hard perception cases. Sell each set by the day with a motion-capture and camera rig, calibrated lighting and a teleop station. Add a local, trained teleoperator pool billed per accepted demonstration hour, plus a QA pipeline that delivers clean, labeled data.
why_now: Humanoid and VLA robotics funding is in a data-collection race in 2026. MIT Technology Review has covered gig workers training humanoids at home, and China's state-backed training centers run 100+ robots at a time. Paxini reportedly owns a 12,000 m2 collection facility, and AGIBOT rents robots with operators for about $500/day. Dead-mall owners are more distressed than ever, and cheap rental of a robot plus an operator means small teams need somewhere to use them.
revenue_model: Day-rate per environment ($1.5-4k/day). Per-accepted-hour teleop data fees. Monthly reserved 'bays' for resident robotics teams. Later, a revenue share when customers license the resulting datasets.
non_obvious_insight: For robot learning, messy variety with cheap labor and no neighbors matters more than lab polish. A dead mall is free set design, and its owner will pay to have anchor-store fixtures hauled away. The scarce asset is environment diversity plus ops discipline, and the mall itself is nearly free.
first_30_days: Contact 10 owners of dead or dying malls within driving distance of robotics clusters (Pittsburgh, Boston, Detroit, Austin, exurban Bay Area, Atlanta). Sign one 6-month license and build 3 sets for under $25k. Pre-sell 3 pilot collection weeks to startups through robotics meetups and founder networks, with $10-15k deposits.
